title: Multirate Systems and Filter Banks
topics: Chapter 1, 1.1 Major Developments: the emergence of decimators and expanders, sampling-rate conversion, subband decomposition, and the computational motivation for multirate DSP.
Chapter 1, 1.1.1 The Quadrature Mirror Filter (QMF) Bank: two-band analysis, decimation, unequal bit allocation, expansion, and synthesis for subband coding.
Chapter 1, 1.1.2 Polyphase Decomposition: reorganizing filters so arithmetic occurs at the lowest available sample rate.
Chapter 1, 1.1.3 Perfect Reconstruction Systems: alias cancellation and amplitude/phase distortion conditions for exact delayed reconstruction.
Chapter 1, 1.1.4 Extension to M Channels: uniform, nonuniform, and octave-band banks and their relation to short-time Fourier analysis.
Chapter 1, 1.1.5 Other Applications and Interrelations: coding, transmultiplexing, A/D conversion, adaptive filtering, equalization, wavelets, and statistical signal processing.
Chapter 1, 1.2 Scope and Outline: the book's progression from fundamentals through two-channel and M-channel perfect-reconstruction banks, paraunitary systems, and multidimensional extensions.
Chapter 2, 2.0 Introduction and 2.1 Discrete-Time Signals: sequence notation, impulses, steps, exponentials, periodicity, and energy/power conventions.
Chapter 2, 2.1.1 Transform Domain Analysis: z-transforms, regions of convergence, Fourier transforms, rational transforms, poles, and zeros.
Chapter 2, 2.1.2 Discrete-Time Systems: linearity, time invariance, convolution, causality, stability, and exponential eigenfunctions.
Chapter 2, 2.1.3 Implementations of Rational Transfer Functions: direct, cascade, parallel, and real second-order-section realizations.
Chapter 2, 2.1.4 Continuous-Time Systems: sampling, spectral replication, aliasing, reconstruction, and baseband/bandpass sampling conditions.
Chapter 2, 2.2 Multi-Input Multi-Output Systems: transfer matrices, vector convolution, MIMO eigenfunction behavior, elementwise stability, and McMillan degree.
Chapter 2, 2.3.1-2.3.2 Preliminaries and Polynomials: complex-variable, matrix, polynomial-degree, coprimeness, and greatest-common-divisor conventions.
Chapter 2, 2.3.3 The Tilde Notation (Paraconjugation): scalar and matrix paraconjugates, reciprocal-conjugate zeros, and analytic extension from the unit circle.
Chapter 2, 2.3.4-2.3.6 Matrices, FIR Functions, and Miscellaneous Symbols: Hermitian/unitary matrices, FIR order and length, and the notation used throughout the book.
Chapter 2, 2.4 Discrete-Time Filters: rational digital filters, magnitude/phase response, group delay, and minimum-/maximum-phase factors.
Chapter 2, 2.4.1 Magnitude Response and Phase Response: amplitude, phase, phase delay, group delay, and phase unwrapping.
Chapter 2, 2.4.2 Linear Phase Filters: the four real FIR linear-phase types, symmetry constraints, forced zeros, and multiplier savings.
Chapter 2, 2.4.3 Analytic Continuation: promoting rational identities that agree on the unit circle to identities in z.
Chapter 2, Problems 2.1-2.15: proofs and computations on transforms, stability, realizations, paraconjugation, linear phase, and matrix systems.
Chapter 3, 3.0 Introduction and 3.1 Filter Design Specifications: passband/stopband tolerances, transition bands, minimax, least-squares, and flatness objectives.
Chapter 3, 3.2.1 Window Design: truncated ideal responses, Gibbs behavior, window mainlobes/sidelobes, and Kaiser and Dolph-Chebyshev windows.
Chapter 3, 3.2.2 The Prolate Sequence—Another Optimal Window: minimum out-of-band energy as a Toeplitz eigenvalue problem.
Chapter 3, 3.2.3 Optimal Lowpass Eigenfilters: weighted passband/stopband least-squares FIR design as a minimum-eigenvector problem.
Chapter 3, 3.2.4 Equiripple FIR Filters: minimax FIR design with Remez/Parks-McClellan exchange.
Chapter 3, 3.2.5 Spectral Factorization: factoring a nonnegative zero-phase FIR response into reciprocal-conjugate factors and selecting minimum phase.
Chapter 3, 3.3 IIR Filter Design: order efficiency and nonlinear-phase tradeoffs.
Chapter 3, 3.3.1 The Bilinear Transformation: stable analog-to-digital mapping, frequency warping, and prewarping.
Chapter 3, 3.3.2 Analog Filters: Butterworth, Chebyshev, inverse-Chebyshev, and elliptic prototypes.
Chapter 3, 3.3.3 Properties of Digital Elliptic Filters: equiripple optimality, pole-zero structure, and order comparisons.
Chapter 3, 3.4.1 Properties of Allpass Functions: reciprocal-conjugate poles and zeros, constant magnitude, energy preservation, and phase monotonicity.
Chapter 3, 3.4.2-3.4.3 Simple and Lattice Structures for Allpass Filters: first-/second-order sections, order reduction, reflection coefficients, and low-sensitivity implementations.
Chapter 3, 3.5 Special Types of Filters: bounded-real, lossless bounded-real, allpass, and power-complementary transfer functions.
Chapter 3, 3.6.1 The Allpass Decomposition Theorem: representing suitable bounded power-complementary IIR pairs as half-sum and half-difference of allpass functions.
Chapter 3, 3.6.2 Elliptic, Butterworth, and Chebyshev Filters: applying allpass decomposition to standard odd-order IIR families and exploiting pole interlacing.
Chapter 3, 3.7 Concluding Remarks and Problems 3.1-3.21: design comparisons plus proof- and implementation-oriented exercises.
Chapter 4, 4.0 Introduction and 4.1.1 Decimation and Interpolation: time- and frequency-domain definitions, imaging, aliasing, and anti-imaging/anti-alias filtering.
Chapter 4, 4.1.2 Digital Filter Banks: analysis/synthesis banks, subband signals, uniform DFT banks, and spectrum-analyzer interpretations.
Chapter 4, 4.1.3 Time Domain Descriptions of Multirate Filters: sample-by-sample equations for filtered rate conversion and rational L/M conversion.
Chapter 4, 4.2 Interconnection of Building Blocks: coprime commutation rules and the two noble identities.
Chapter 4, 4.3 The Polyphase Representation: Type 1 and Type 2 decompositions and their matrix/vector interpretations.
Chapter 4, 4.3.1 Efficient Structures for Decimation and Interpolation Filters: moving polyphase filters to the low-rate side and exploiting FIR symmetry.
Chapter 4, 4.3.2 Polyphase Implementation of Uniform DFT Filter Banks: a prototype's polyphase components followed or preceded by a DFT.
Chapter 4, 4.3.3 Efficient Structures for Fractional Decimation: coprime rearrangement and all arithmetic at the lowest rate.
Chapter 4, 4.3.4-4.3.5 Commutator Models and Further Applications: rotating-switch models, periodically time-varying behavior, and a simple perfect-reconstruction DFT bank.
Chapter 4, 4.4.1 The Interpolated FIR (IFIR) Approach: a stretched model filter plus an image suppressor for efficient narrowband FIR design.
Chapter 4, 4.4.2 Multistage Design of Decimation and Interpolation Filters: factoring large conversion ratios and distributing transition bands across stages.
Chapter 4, 4.5.1-4.5.5 Applications: digital audio, speech/image subband coding, voice privacy, transmultiplexers, and multirate adaptive filters.
Chapter 4, 4.6.1 M-th Band or Nyquist(M) Filters: periodic impulse-response zeros, shifted-response sums, half-band filters, and window/eigenfilter design.
Chapter 4, 4.6.2 Complementary Transfer Functions: strictly, power, allpass, doubly, and Euclidean complementary families.
Chapter 4, 4.6.3 Relation Between Nyquist(M) Filters and Power Complementary Filters: equivalence between an M-th-band product and power-complementary polyphase components.
Chapter 4, 4.6.4 Applications of Special Transfer Functions: reconstruction, interpolation, digital crossovers, and hybrid digital/analog filter banks.
Chapter 4, 4.6.5 Adjustable Multilevel Filters and Tunable Filters: shifted Nyquist prototypes, polyphase implementation, independent band levels, and discrete cutoff tuning.
Chapter 4, 4.7.1-4.7.3 Multigrid Foundations: discretized differential equations, stationary iterations, residual/error dynamics, and the stalling phenomenon.
Chapter 4, 4.7.4 Basic Idea of the Multigrid Approach: residual smoothing, decimation to a coarse grid, interpolation of an error correction, and the Galerkin coarse-grid matrix.
Chapter 4, Problems 4.1-4.33: spectral sketches, rate-changing identities, polyphase derivations, arithmetic counts, IFIR and complementary-filter designs, and multigrid proofs.
key_results: Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1: multirate processing adds decimators and expanders to ordinary DSP primitives so computation, transmission rate, and storage can be reduced without merely throwing information away.

Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1.1: in a two-band QMF coder, the average rate is one half the sum of the low- and high-band word lengths; assigning more bits to the perceptually or statistically important band yields compression.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1.3: a two-channel analysis/synthesis bank has the form Xhat(z)=T(z)X(z)+alias terms; perfect reconstruction requires all alias terms to vanish and T(z)=c z^-K.
Chapter 1, Secs. 1.1.2-1.1.4: polyphase decomposition is the structural mechanism that lets M-channel filtering run near the decimated rates rather than redundantly at the input rate.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.1: a z-transform expression alone does not uniquely specify a sequence; its region of convergence is essential, and the DTFT exists when the unit circle lies in that region.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.2: complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: input a^n produces H(a)a^n whenever the relevant transforms converge.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.2: a discrete LTI system is causal exactly when h(n)=0 for n<0 and BIBO-stable exactly when h is absolutely summable; a causal rational system is stable exactly when every pole is inside the unit circle.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.3: the minimum number of delays needed to realize a scalar rational transfer function equals its order; real filters can be implemented as real first- and second-order cascade sections.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.4: uniform sampling replicates the analog spectrum every 2pi/T; a signal limited to |Omega|<sigma can be recovered at sampling rate at least 2sigma, while certain bandpass signals admit lower rates under nonoverlap constraints.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.2: for a MIMO LTI system, a vector exponential v a^n is mapped to H(a)v a^n; causality and stability reduce to the corresponding property of every scalar matrix entry.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.2: the McMillan degree of a rational transfer matrix is the smallest number of delays among all its realizations, generalizing scalar filter order.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3.3: paraconjugation H~(z)=H*(1/z*) analytically extends conjugation on the unit circle; for matrices it also transposes, and H~H continues |H|^2 away from the unit circle.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3.3: paraconjugation replaces each zero by its reciprocal conjugate and exchanges minimum- and maximum-phase factors.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4.2: the four real FIR linear-phase types arise from symmetry versus antisymmetry and even versus odd order; the type determines forced zeros at omega=0 and/or pi, while coefficient pairing nearly halves multipliers.

Chapter 2, Secs. 2.4.2-2.4.3: a generalized-Hermitian rational function has linear phase on the unit circle; analytic continuation lets unit-circle equalities be treated as rational identities, and a causal stable rational linear-phase filter must be FIR.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.1: truncating the ideal sinc response gives a least-squares approximation, but increasing length narrows the Gibbs ripples without reducing their peak; a better window trades sidelobe height against mainlobe width.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.1: the Kaiser window exposes a practical two-parameter design: beta is selected mainly by desired attenuation and order N mainly by transition width.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.2: the discrete prolate sequence minimizes out-of-band energy under unit norm and is the principal eigenvector of a real symmetric positive-definite Toeplitz matrix; the optimum is unique and symmetric.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.3: the optimal lowpass eigenfilter is the unit-norm eigenvector associated with the smallest eigenvalue of a weighted positive-definite matrix R assembled from passband and stopband errors.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.4: Parks-McClellan/Remez design produces the minimum-order real linear-phase FIR response for a prescribed minimax equiripple specification, including unequal passband and stopband weights.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.5: a nonnegative zero-phase FIR response factors as H(z)=H0~(z)H0(z); choosing one zero from each reciprocal-conjugate pair produces the minimum-phase factor, unique up to a unit-magnitude constant.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.5: spectral factorization can yield a nonlinear-phase FIR filter of roughly half the zero-phase order, but the intermediate squared-magnitude design may need about twice the requested attenuation and can be numerically delicate.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.1: the bilinear map s=(1-z^-1)/(1+z^-1) maps the stable analog half-plane to the inside of the unit circle and relates analog and digital frequencies by Omega=tan(omega/2), requiring edge prewarping.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.2: an Nth-order Butterworth magnitude-squared response is maximally flat through derivative order 2N-1 at zero frequency and rolls off asymptotically at 20N dB per decade.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.3: elliptic filters are minimax among rational filters with prescribed orders and band edges; equiripple error in both bands can reduce order dramatically compared with Butterworth or linear-phase FIR designs.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.1: H is allpass with gain c exactly when H~(z)H(z)=c^2; poles and zeros occur in reciprocal-conjugate pairs, a stable causal allpass preserves signal energy up to c^2, and its impulse autocorrelation is c^2 delta(n).
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.1: an Nth-order stable causal allpass has monotonically decreasing unwrapped phase with total change 2pi N around the unit circle.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.3: repeatedly extracting a reflection coefficient reduces a stable unit allpass to a lattice; |k_m|<1 at every stage is equivalent to stability, so quantization that preserves those bounds also preserves stability and the allpass property.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.6.1: a suitable real bounded power-complementary pair with symmetric/antisymmetric numerators is the half-sum and half-difference of two stable unit allpass functions whose orders add to the original order.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.6.2: odd-order Butterworth, Chebyshev, and elliptic filters meet the allpass-decomposition conditions; their interlaced pole subsets make two-output implementations possible with roughly N multipliers total.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.1: expansion by L compresses the spectrum and creates L images, whereas decimation by M stretches and sums M shifted spectra; spectral overlap in that sum is aliasing.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.1: the standard L/M converter expands by L, lowpass-filters, then decimates by M; the common filter both removes interpolation images and prevents decimation aliasing.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.2: a uniform DFT analysis bank can be generated from one prototype H0(z) by Hk(z)=H0(zW^k); the delay-chain/DFT interpretation connects filter banks to sliding short-time Fourier analysis.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.2: an L-fold expander and M-fold decimator commute exactly when L and M are relatively prime.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.2: the noble identities move a rational filter G(z^M) across an M-fold rate changer, converting high-rate filtering into the equivalent low-rate operation.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3: every H(z) has Type 1 polyphase form H(z)=sum_{l=0}^{M-1} z^-l E_l(z^M); Type 2 contains the same components in a different cyclic ordering.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.1: an M-fold polyphase decimator performs filtering after downsampling and saves approximately a factor M in arithmetic; the dual interpolator avoids all multiplies on inserted zeros.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.2: an M-channel DFT bank needs only the prototype's polyphase subfilters plus one M-point DFT rather than M separate full-rate filters.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.3: when L and M are coprime, the fractional converter can be rearranged so every polyphase computation occurs at the lower internal rate; its arithmetic per output is essentially independent of L.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.5: multirate systems are generally linear periodically time-varying, but alias cancellation can make an overall analysis/synthesis system LTI; a simple DFT-bank construction reconstructs a scaled delayed input exactly.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.4.1: IFIR realizes a narrowband filter as G(z^M1) followed by an image suppressor I(z); stretching reduces model-filter order while the suppressor removes the newly created passband images.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.4.2: a large rate change should often be factored into stages so early filters operate at favorable rates and later filters see relaxed transition specifications; the best factorization balances per-stage orders and rates.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.1: H is Nyquist(M) when one polyphase component is a monomial, equivalently its impulse response has periodic zero crossings and its M uniformly shifted frequency responses sum to a constant.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.1: a real zero-phase FIR half-band lowpass has equal passband/stopband ripple, band edges symmetric about pi/2, and an impulse-response length constrained to 4J+3 in the nontrivial case.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.2: power complementarity means sum_k |Hk(e^jomega)|^2=c and supports exact reconstruction with paraconjugate synthesis filters; an FIR complementary mate can be obtained by spectral-factorizing 1-|H0|^2.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.2: relatively prime FIR analysis filters are Euclidean complementary, so Bezout synthesis polynomials exist for causal FIR exact reconstruction, although poor scaling can make the construction numerically impractical.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.3: the M polyphase components of H(z) are power complementary if and only if G(z)=H~(z)H(z) is Nyquist(M).

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.5: adjustable multilevel filters are weighted sums of M shifted versions of one Nyquist(M) prototype; the Nyquist shifted-sum property prevents bumps and dips between independently tunable band levels.

Chapter 4, Secs. 4.7.2-4.7.3: for y_{k+1}=Py_k+q with P=I-alpha A, residual and error obey r_k=P^k r_0 and e_k=P^k e_0; stalling is domination by the eigenmode whose eigenvalue has the largest magnitude.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.7.4: when the iteration operator behaves like a lowpass filter, high-frequency residual modes die first and the stalled residual is smooth enough to decimate to a coarser grid.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.7.4: multigrid solves a smaller coarse-grid error equation, interpolates that error to the fine grid, and corrects the stalled estimate; the coarse operator is chosen as A^(2Delta)=M_D A^(Delta) M_I.
pedagogy: A mathematically mature, theorem-and-structure-oriented treatment that deliberately builds a reusable notation before the main multirate material. Chapter 1 motivates the field through systems and applications; Chapters 2-3 are concise reviews but still state the algebraic facts needed later, while Chapter 4 alternates transform derivations, sample-level arguments, block-diagram identities, operation counts, and concrete designs. Proofs are often given immediately after a claim—especially for polyphase equivalences, complementary functions, allpass structure, and the multigrid connection—and important qualifications are surfaced through counterexamples or warnings. The presentation assumes prior signals-and-systems fluency, complex algebra, z-transforms, Fourier analysis, matrices/eigenvalues, and basic filter design; the multigrid section also expects elementary differential equations and numerical linear algebra but explicitly favors concepts over rigor. Worked examples carry real specifications through order and cost estimates, including Kaiser, elliptic, fractional-rate, DFT-bank, IFIR, and multistage designs. The exercises are unusually strong: 15 in Chapter 2, 21 in Chapter 3, and 33 in Chapter 4, dominated by derivations and proofs but also requiring spectral sketches, explicit coefficients, structure drawings, rate/operation accounting, design optimization, and numerical experiments. Several hard problems are intentionally used to complete proofs or design procedures only outlined in the prose.

gems: Chapter 1's oversampled audio example makes the analog/digital bargain concrete: sample at twice the eventual rate behind a gentler analog anti-alias filter, perform a sharp linear-phase digital filter, then decimate.

The historical audio rates—48 kHz studio, 44.1 kHz compact disc, and 32 kHz broadcast—turn abstract rational rate conversion into the demanding 48-to-44.1 kHz interface later revisited as L=441, M=480.
The extreme QMF bit-allocation thought experiment assigns all bits to the lowpass channel when the input is overwhelmingly lowpass, making perceptual/statistical compression visible in one equation.
The text treats an M-channel filter bank as a generalization of a short-block Fourier analyzer, a compact conceptual bridge between filter-bank spectra and transform methods.
The paraconjugate notation looks cosmetic at first, then becomes the language that unifies magnitude squares, reciprocal-conjugate zeros, allpass filters, and power complementarity.

A zero-phase ideal lowpass truncated to greater length gets a narrower transition but stubbornly retains roughly the same Gibbs peak—an excellent corrective to the intuition that more taps fix every error.
Design Example 3.2.1 turns omega_p=0.2pi, omega_s=0.3pi, and 40 dB attenuation into a Kaiser beta of about 3.395 and order about 46, clearly separating the roles of attenuation and transition width.
The prolate sequence and eigenfilter are dual-looking eigenproblems: maximize in-band window energy with the largest eigenvalue, but minimize filter approximation error with the smallest eigenvalue.

For one specification, the book contrasts elliptic order 7, Butterworth order 28, and linear-phase equiripple FIR order 101; the cost advantage is dramatic, but the elliptic group delay varies roughly from 10 to 60 samples.

A 7th-order elliptic pair implemented through two allpass branches needs 7 multipliers and 22 adders versus 11 and 14 in a direct implementation, showing why multiply count alone does not decide the best structure.
The rational 3/2 rate-converter example needs only about an 11th-order linear-phase filter for its stated 0.01 ripple, and polyphase symmetry reduces this to six multipliers.

A 32-channel, order-50 DFT bank falls from roughly 1,632 multiplications in direct filtering to 187 using polyphase-plus-DFT structure; after decimation, the prototype filtering costs only about six real multiplications per input interval.

The simple DFT filter bank formed from delay chains is exactly perfect-reconstruction despite its crude roughly 13 dB channel selectivity: it returns M^2 x(n-M+1), separating reconstruction algebra from subband quality.
In the IFIR example, a direct order-233 linear-phase filter using 117 multipliers is replaced by a stretched order-131 model plus order-6 image suppressor using 70 multipliers.

The 50-fold 8 kHz-to-160 Hz decimator drops from an estimated order 2028 and about 21 million multiplies/s to a multistage design with orders 90 and 139 and about 3.72 million multiplies/s—roughly a sixfold saving.
A subband-coding example compresses a 10 ksample/s, 16-bit stream from 160 kb/s to 120 kb/s simply by splitting into two critically decimated bands and assigning 16 versus 8 bits.
The voice-privacy system is almost mischievously simple: split speech into bands, permute them in frequency and optionally in time, then invert the permutation for authorized recovery.

Euclidean complementarity promises causal FIR exact reconstruction from relatively prime analysis filters, then immediately warns that the unique low-degree synthesis pair can be oppositely selective and so poorly scaled that quantization overwhelms the reconstruction constant.

The woofer/tweeter crossover example distinguishes allpass complementarity from power complementarity: an undistorted sum does not by itself guarantee that the second branch is a good highpass, so doubly complementary filters solve two different engineering requirements.
The phrase polyphase is explained physically: each decimated phase approximates a fractional phase ramp e^(j omega l/M), and the M nearly equal-magnitude terms align in the prototype passband.

Multigrid appears in a signal-processing text because a stalled residual is often smooth: stationary iteration behaves like lowpass filtering, so the stubborn error is precisely the part that can be represented cheaply on a coarser sampled grid.

Problem 4.30 packages an efficient half-band design trick: design a Type 2 one-band equiripple filter at half the final order, substitute z^2, add a delay, and obtain the alternating zeros and nonnegative response required later for perfect-reconstruction banks.
chapter_map: Field motivation, QMF history, polyphase and perfect-reconstruction preview, M-channel extensions, and the book roadmap -> Chapter 1, Secs. 1.1-1.2 (book pp. 1-11).

Discrete-time and continuous-time review; z-transform/ROC, LTI and MIMO systems, paraconjugation, rational realizations, and four FIR linear-phase types -> Chapter 2, Secs. 2.0-2.4 plus Problems 2.1-2.15.

FIR design by windows, prolate sequences, eigenfilters, equiripple approximation, and spectral factorization; IIR design, allpass theory/lattices, and allpass decomposition -> Chapter 3, Secs. 3.0-3.7 plus Problems 3.1-3.21.

Decimation/interpolation, rate-changing identities, polyphase and DFT-bank implementations, IFIR and multistage designs, applications, Nyquist/complementary filters, tunable multilevel filters, and multigrid -> Chapter 4, Secs. 4.0-4.7 plus Problems 4.1-4.33, ending at book p. 187.
